raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Overview Adds `--max-async-kv-loads-per-step` (default `None`), which limits how many async KV loads one `schedule()` may start. #65319 (merged) bounds how many loads are held at once; this bounds how fast they start. The two solve different problems on a DP decode instance, where every rank waits for the slowest rank's step. Merged with main and tested at `8d2b491533` (main at `226104db52`, 2026-11-04). The limit now shares its gate with the in-flight cap. ## Claims - **Hard bound per step.** With the cap alone, one step can start up to `cap - held` loads. On one real `schedule()` with 140K-token requests, that is 42.7 ms at cap 16 and 174.3 ms at cap 64, against 5.8 ms at cap 64 with a limit of 2. - **No cap value does both jobs.** The cap must exceed rate x load time or requests fall behind. At the highest load tested, caps 16 and 32 wait 20 s and 8 s, while caps of 64 and above keep up and still start 32 loads in one step. - **The limit fixes that without falling behind.** In the same high-load case, the slowest rank's `schedule()` goes from 28.7 / 48.2 ms (mean / p99) at cap 64 to 14.6 / 14.6 ms at limit 4 and 9.0 / 9.0 ms at limit 2, while the wait before a load starts goes from 0.05 s to 0.07 s and 0.17 s. - **The limit has its own range.** It must stay above the arrival rate and at or below the typical burst. Limit 1 falls behind at 1.43 req/step. At the reference load with bursts of 2, limit 4 gains almost nothing and limits 1-2 help. - **The cap does not need to be large.** Beyond keeping up, a larger cap only moves the queue behind the transfer. Peak finished loads waiting for a slot reaches 231 per rank at cap 256 under overload, against 14 at cap 16. These hold KV blocks and add to every step. - **Not shown yet:** GPU idle time or throughput for the combination. There is no E2E run of cap + per-step limit. ## Validation ### CPU-only repro Drives the real `Scheduler` and NIXL scheduler-side connector at `8d2b491533`, using the real `--max-async-kv-loads-per-step` and `--max-num-inflight-kv-loads` settings. Only the GPU and the transfer are faked: a load finishes a fixed 30 steps after it starts. All configs in a scenario see the same arrival stream. ```bash # From a checkout of this PR, with native extensions available. # Reads the facebook/opt-125m HF config. Each scenario takes several minutes. PYTHONPATH=. python repro_per_step_vs_inflight.py --jobs 8 2>/dev/null PYTHONPATH=. python repro_per_step_vs_inflight.py --jobs 8 --skip-part1 --scale 4 --burst 8 --steps 2000 --warmup 800 2>/dev/null ``` **Part 1: one real `schedule()`, measured.** 64 queued 140K-token requests on an idle rank, 8,750 blocks per request, one call per config, aarch64 host. | Config | Loads started | `schedule()` | |---|---:|---:| | cap 16 | 16 | 42.7 ms | | cap 64 | 64 | 174.3 ms | | cap 64, per-step 2 | 2 | 5.8 ms | **Part 2: 16 DP ranks.** Load counts come from the real scheduler. Milliseconds are modeled from the reference run as 3.4 ms + 2.8 ms x loads started, taking the rank that started the most each step. Warmup steps are discarded. "Backlog / rank at end" is the average number of requests per rank that have arrived but not started their KV load at the last step, a snapshot that keeps growing with run length when a config falls behind arrivals. **High-load showcase (synthetic).** `--scale 4 --burst 8`: `max-num-seqs` 512, 1.43 req/step/rank in bursts of 8, 2,000 steps. Rate x load time = 43. This is not a measured deployment: `max-num-seqs`, rate and burst are scaled up from the reference run, and the 2.8 ms per load is carried over unchanged. | Config | Max loads in a step | Steps with >=3 loads | Slowest rank mean (ms) | Slowest rank p99 (ms) | Wait before load (s) | Backlog / rank at end | Peak finished loads waiting | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | main default (no limits) | 128 | 92.4% | 31.4 | 138.0 | 0.03 | 5.5 | 100 | | per-step 6 only | 6 | 97.8% | 19.9 | 20.2 | 0.05 | 6.1 | 94 | | cap 16 | 8 | 56.7% | 16.1 | 25.8 | 19.86 | 1725.5 | 0 | | cap 32 | 16 | 90.0% | 25.1 | 48.2 | 7.72 | 661.0 | 0 | | cap 48 | 24 | 93.9% | 28.6 | 48.2 | 0.39 | 25.5 | 15 | | cap 64 | 32 | 94.7% | 28.7 | 48.2 | 0.05 | 6.6 | 32 | | cap 256 | 32 | 93.8% | 28.8 | 48.4 | 0.00 | 0.0 | 105 | | **cap 64, per-step 4** | 4 | 100.0% | 14.6 | 14.6 | 0.07 | 8.4 | 31 | | cap 64, per-step 3 | 3 | 100.0% | 11.8 | 11.8 | 0.09 | 10.4 | 30 | | **cap 64, per-step 2** | 2 | 0.0% | 9.0 | 9.0 | 0.17 | 17.6 | 30 | | cap 64, per-step 1 | 1 | 0.0% | 6.2 | 6.2 | 9.31 | 802.4 | 0 | Low caps and per-step 1 look fast here only because they start fewer loads than arrive. **At the reference load.** `max-num-seqs` 128, 0.358 req/step/rank, bursts of 2, 3,000 steps. Rate x load time = 10.7. The gain is much smaller here. | Config | Max loads in a step | Steps with >=3 loads | Slowest rank mean (ms) | Slowest rank p99 (ms) | Wait before load (s) | Backlog / rank at end | Peak finished loads waiting | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | main default (no limits) | 38 | 20.0% | 11.0 | 65.0 | 0.07 | 2.2 | 30 | | per-step 6, as in the reference run | 6 | 24.9% | 10.6 | 20.2 | 0.07 | 4.1 | 27 | | cap 4 | 2 | 0.0% | 6.6 | 9.0 | 28.43 | 661.1 | 0 | | cap 8 | 4 | 6.7% | 8.8 | 14.6 | 10.97 | 262.1 | 0 | | cap 12 | 8 | 15.8% | 9.6 | 14.6 | 0.42 | 12.7 | 9 | | cap 16 | 8 | 16.8% | 9.7 | 14.6 | 0.08 | 4.6 | 13 | | cap 64 | 8 | 18.7% | 9.8 | 20.2 | 0.00 | 0.0 | 32 | | cap 16, per-step 4 | 4 | 17.1% | 9.6 | 14.6 | 0.08 | 4.6 | 13 | | cap 16, per-step 3 | 3 | 18.8% | 9.2 | 11.8 | 0.08 | 4.6 | 13 | | **cap 16, per-step 2** | 2 | 0.0% | 8.8 | 9.0 | 0.08 | 4.6 | 13 | | **cap 16, per-step 1** | 1 | 0.0% | 6.2 | 6.2 | 0.10 | 5.2 | 13 | **Sensitivity.** Mean / p99 of the slowest rank's `schedule()`, in ms. Burst size is an assumption and the gain depends on it. Bursts of 2 were picked for the reference load because the per-step 6 row (10.6 ms) is closest to the 10.9 ms measured. Burst size per step has not been measured directly. | Scenario | Cap alone | Cap, per-step 4 | Cap, per-step 2 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `max-num-seqs` 128, cap 16, Poisson (`--burst 1`) | 7.9 / 11.8 | 7.9 / 11.8 | 7.7 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 128, cap 16, `--burst 2` | 9.7 / 14.6 | 9.6 / 14.6 | 8.8 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 128, cap 16, `--burst 4` | 12.0 / 25.8 | 11.7 / 14.6 | 8.7 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 128, cap 16, overload (`--burst 4 --rate 0.45`) | 8.9 / 14.6 | 8.9 / 14.6 | 8.1 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 512, cap 64, `--burst 2` | 17.4 / 31.4 | 14.3 / 14.6 | 9.0 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 512, cap 64, `--burst 4` | 21.4 / 37.0 | 14.6 / 14.6 | 9.0 / 9.0 | | `max-num-seqs` 512, cap 64, `--burst 8` | 28.7 / 48.2 | 14.6 / 14.6 | 9.0 / 9.0 | With pure Poisson arrivals at the reference load the limit only trims the tail. In the overload run, wait before a load is not lost time: requests are queueing for running slots anyway, and cap 256 only moves that queue behind the transfer (peak finished loads waiting 231).
Reference run DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, AgentX, 8 prefill instances (DEP2) and 1 decode instance (DEP16), concurrency 6600, `max-num-seqs` 128, per-step limit 6, no in-flight cap. One hour, with lightweight CPU hooks on all 16 decode ranks and CUDA events on the worker's main stream. Average prompt ~140K tokens. - GPU step 23.1 ms, of which 1.9 ms (8%) is the GPU waiting on the CPU. Wait before forward launch: p50 0.2 ms, p90 6 ms, p99 20 ms. - 1.1 ms of that 1.9 ms is `execute_model`'s per-step DP batch-size all-reduce waiting for the slowest rank. - The last rank to reach the all-reduce is 10.5 ms behind the median rank on average (p90 21 ms). Its `schedule()` takes 10.9 ms (median rank 3.5 ms) and its `update_from_output()` 4.4 ms (1.1 ms). All 16 ranks are slowest about equally often. - `schedule()` takes 3.4 ms (p50) with no new load and ~2.8 ms more per load started: 20.5 ms at 6 loads. `update_from_output()` takes 0.9 ms with no finished request and ~2.3 ms more per finished request. - ~15.5 req/s per rank (~0.36 per step), ~0.69 s per KV load.
### E2E, before #65319 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, 7 prefill instances (DEP2) and 1 decode instance (DEP16), NIXL, AgentX at concurrency 4800, with the decode batch full: | | tok/s/GPU | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | |---|---:|---:| | no limit | 460K | 109 | | limit 4 | 516K | 153 | The decode step returned to the decode-only level (22.4 ms). These runs came from a development tree and included two smaller CPU fixes on the same admission path, so not all of the gain belongs to this change. Limit 4 beat 10-12 there. Before #65319 the limit was also the only thing holding back the pile-up of finished loads, a job the cap now does. ### Unit tests ```bash pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_kv_load_failure_recovery.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -q pre-commit run --files vllm/config/scheduler.py vllm/engine/arg_utils.py vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py ``` 324 passed on CPU, and pre-commit passes. `test_max_async_kv_loads_per_step` covers the limit alone, with the cap, and with the cap on a full batch. Restoring the previous check (`self.waiting` only) fails the two cap cases; removing the limit fails all three. This change only affects scheduling order, not model output, so there are no accuracy evals. ## Details **How a burst becomes a GPU stall:** 1. Prefill finishes and the request reaches a decode rank's waiting queue. 2. `schedule()` starts its async KV load: it allocates KV blocks for the whole prompt and moves it to `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`. It takes no running slot, so nothing but the cap limits how many start in one step. 3. Each load costs ~2.8 ms of Python on that rank. 4. The next `execute_model` does a DP all-reduce, so all 16 ranks wait for the rank that started the most. 5. The KV arrives, and the request waits for a running slot. **Why the cap alone leaves this open.** The cap only binds once `held` nears `cap`, and `cap` has to stay above rate x load time to keep up. In the reference run about 2/3 of the time was spent below `max-num-seqs`, with ~10.6 loads in progress, so a cap large enough to keep up leaves room for a burst. When the batch is full and the cap is reached, #65319 already paces loads to one per admission, and the limit adds little there. #65319's description also notes that a per-step limit could be layered on. **Implementation.** With a cap set, remote-prefill requests wait in `async_kv_waiting`, so the limit moved from a `self.waiting` check before the head is peeked to the gate shared with `_admits_inflight_kv_load()`. A head stopped by the limit behaves like one stopped by the cap: an `async_kv_waiting` head stops only that queue for the step, and a `self.waiting` head ends admission for the step. Each limited step still evaluates one head request up to that gate, as the cap already does. **Suggested settings, from this repro only:** cap around 1.5x rate x load time (16 at the reference load), and a per-step limit above the arrival rate and no larger than the typical burst. This depends on load, so the limit is a setting and not a fixed default. **Limitations:** - The repro models `schedule()` on the slowest rank, not GPU idle, and leaves out `update_from_output()`. Its numbers are not a predicted bubble reduction, and async overlap absorbs part of a late rank. - Step time does not feed back into arrivals. Load time is fixed at 30 steps, and the arrival process is synthetic. - Raising concurrency alone does not reach the high-load case. Once prefill is saturated, decode's arrival rate stops growing; it takes more prefill capacity and a larger `max-num-seqs`. - Even at limit 1, some rank starts a load on most steps, so the slowest rank stays near 6.2 ms. Lowering that needs a lower cost per load. - #64379 and #65285 (both open) remove the repeated reservation sum. Part 1 is already linear at this size (~2.7 ms per load), so they would not remove this per-load cost. **Not a duplicate:** searched open PRs for `per-step async kv` and `max_num_inflight_kv_loads`. #65319 caps loads held, and its description lists this change as an alternative and a possible layer on top. #64379 and #65285 lower the cost of an admission, not how many start in a step.
repro_per_step_vs_inflight.py ```python #!/usr/bin/env python """Why --max-num-inflight-kv-loads (#65319) still needs a per-step limit (#61725). CPU only. Drives the real Scheduler and NIXL scheduler-side connector; only the GPU and the transfer are faked (a load finishes `--load-steps` later). Usage, from a checkout of #61725: PYTHONPATH=. python repro_per_step_vs_inflight.py 2>/dev/null Part 1 times a real schedule() call: one step can start `cap` loads. Part 2 replays 16 DP ranks. A rank that parks N loads delays every rank, because each step's DP all-reduce waits for the slowest one. """ import argparse import logging import multiprocessing as mp import os import random import time os.environ.setdefault("HF_HUB_DISABLE_PROGRESS_BARS", "1") import numpy as np from tests.v1.kv_connector.unit.utils import ( create_model_runner_output, create_request, create_scheduler, create_vllm_config, ) from vllm.v1.metrics.stats import ( KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING, KV_FETCH_IN_PROGRESS, ) # Reference: DSv4.1 8P1D DEP16 AgentX c6600, mns 128, per-step 6, 1 h CPU hooks. # Used only to set the load and to turn parked loads into milliseconds. DP_RANKS = 16 MAX_NUM_SEQS = 128 STEP_MS = 23.1 ARRIVALS_PER_STEP = 0.358 # 15.5 req/s per rank LOAD_STEPS = 30 # 0.69 s MEAN_OUTPUT_TOKENS = 320 # 116 running / 0.358 per step SCHEDULE_BASE_MS = 3.4 SCHEDULE_MS_PER_PARK = 2.8 REAL_RUN = "real run, per-step 6: slowest rank's schedule() averages 10.9 ms" def make_configs(scale): """(label, --max-num-inflight-kv-loads, per-step limit); caps scale with load.""" caps = {c: c * scale for c in (4, 8, 12, 16, 64, 256)} return [ ("main default (no limits)", None, None), ("#61725 per-step 6, as run", None, 6), *((f"#65319 cap {caps[c]}", caps[c], None) for c in (4, 8, 12, 16, 64)), *( (f"both: cap {caps[16]}, per-step {k}", caps[16], k) for k in (4, 3, 2, 1) ), (f"both: cap {caps[64]}, per-step 2", caps[64], 2), (f"both: cap {caps[256]}, per-step 2", caps[256], 2), ] def make_rank( cap, per_step, scale=1, block_size=16, num_blocks=60_000, max_len=200_000 ): config = create_vllm_config( max_num_seqs=MAX_NUM_SEQS * scale, max_num_batched_tokens=10 * MAX_NUM_SEQS * scale, block_size=block_size, max_model_len=max_len, ) config.scheduler_config.max_num_inflight_kv_loads = cap config.scheduler_config.max_async_kv_loads_per_step = per_step rank = create_scheduler(config, num_blocks=num_blocks) rank.started = [] set_stage = rank._set_kv_fetch_stage def recording_set_stage(request, stage): if stage == KV_FETCH_IN_PROGRESS: rank.started.append(request) set_stage(request, stage) rank._set_kv_fetch_stage = recording_set_stage return rank def remote_request(num_tokens, max_tokens, block_size=16): return create_request( block_size=block_size, num_tokens=num_tokens, max_tokens=max_tokens, do_remote_prefill=True, num_remote_blocks=num_tokens // block_size, ) def part1_real_schedule_time(num_requests=64, prompt_tokens=140_000): """One real schedule() with a queue of 140K-token requests on an idle rank.""" print(f"\n[Part 1] {num_requests} queued {prompt_tokens // 1000}K-token requests") print(f"{'config':<28}{'loads started':>15}{'schedule() ms':>15}") blocks = (num_requests + 2) * prompt_tokens // 16 for label, cap, per_step in ( ("#65319 cap 16", 16, None), ("#65319 cap 64", 64, None), ("both: cap 64, per-step 2", 64, 2), ): rank = make_rank(cap, per_step, num_blocks=blocks) for _ in range(num_requests): rank.add_request(remote_request(prompt_tokens, 16)) start = time.perf_counter() rank.schedule() elapsed_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1e3 print(f"{label:<28}{len(rank.started):>15}{elapsed_ms:>15.1f}") def arrival_stream(seed, steps, burst, rate): """Poisson arrivals of fixed-size bursts, the same stream for every config.""" rng = random.Random(seed) arrivals = np.random.default_rng(seed).poisson(rate / burst, steps) * burst return [ [1 + int(rng.expovariate(1 / MEAN_OUTPUT_TOKENS)) for _ in range(n)] for n in arrivals ] def replay(args_tuple): """Replay one config on DP_RANKS ranks. Returns one row of the Part 2 table.""" (label, cap, per_step), args = args_tuple parks = np.zeros((args.steps, DP_RANKS), dtype=int) holding_finished = np.zeros((args.steps, DP_RANKS), dtype=int) waits, backlog = [], 0 for r in range(DP_RANKS): rank = make_rank(cap, per_step, args.scale) arrived_at, finishes_at = {}, {} stream = arrival_stream(r, args.steps, args.burst, args.rate) for step, output_lens in enumerate(stream): for max_tokens in output_lens: request = remote_request(160, max_tokens) arrived_at[request.request_id] = step rank.add_request(request) rank.started = [] output = rank.schedule() parks[step, r] = len(rank.started) for request in rank.started: if step >= args.warmup: waits.append(step - arrived_at[request.request_id]) due = step + args.load_steps finishes_at.setdefault(due, set()).add(request.request_id) holding_finished[step, r] = rank._kv_fetch_counts[ KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING ] rank.update_from_output( output, create_model_runner_output( list(rank.running), finished_recving=finishes_at.pop(step + 1, None), ), ) backlog += len(rank.waiting) + len(rank.async_kv_waiting) slowest = parks[args.warmup :].max(axis=1) slowest_ms = SCHEDULE_BASE_MS + SCHEDULE_MS_PER_PARK * slowest return ( label, int(slowest.max()), 100 * float((slowest >= 3).mean()), float(slowest_ms.mean()), float(np.percentile(slowest_ms, 99)), STEP_MS / 1e3 * float(np.mean(waits)) if waits else 0.0, backlog / DP_RANKS, int(holding_finished[args.warmup :].max()), ) def part2_dp_replay(args): needed = args.rate * args.load_steps print( f"\n[Part 2] {DP_RANKS} ranks, mns {MAX_NUM_SEQS * args.scale}, " f"{args.rate:.3f} req/step/rank in bursts of " f"{args.burst}, load {args.load_steps} steps, {args.steps} steps" f"\nCap must exceed rate x load time = {needed:.1f} to keep up." f"\nSlowest rank's schedule() = {SCHEDULE_BASE_MS} + " f"{SCHEDULE_MS_PER_PARK} ms x parks ({REAL_RUN})." ) print( f"{'config':<28}{'max parks':>10}{'steps >=3':>11}{'mean ms':>9}" f"{'p99 ms':>8}{'wait s':>8}{'backlog':>9}{'finished':>10}" ) print( f"{'':<28}{'in a step':>10}{'parks':>11}{'slowest':>9}{'slowest':>8}" f"{'to load':>8}{'/rank':>9}{'waiting':>10}" ) jobs = [(config, args) for config in make_configs(args.scale)] with mp.get_context("fork").Pool(min(args.jobs, len(jobs))) as pool: for row in pool.imap(replay, jobs): print( f"{row[0]:<28}{row[1]:>10}{row[2]:>10.1f}%{row[3]:>9.1f}" f"{row[4]:>8.1f}{row[5]:>8.2f}{row[6]:>9.1f}{row[7]:>10}", flush=True, ) if __name__ == "__main__": parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0]) parser.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=3000) parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=1000) parser.add_argument("--rate", type=float) parser.add_argument( "--scale", type=int, default=1, help="Multiply max-num-seqs, arrival rate and caps: same D utilization.", ) parser.add_argument("--burst", type=int, default=2) parser.add_argument("--load-steps", type=int, default=LOAD_STEPS) parser.add_argument("--jobs", type=int, default=10) parser.add_argument("--skip-part1", action="store_true") cli_args = parser.parse_args() cli_args.rate = cli_args.rate or ARRIVALS_PER_STEP * cli_args.scale logging.disable(logging.WARNING) if not cli_args.skip_part1: part1_real_schedule_time() part2_dp_replay(cli_args) ```

In the overload run, wait before a load is not lost time: requests are queueing for running slots anyway, and cap 256 only moves that queue behind the transfer (peak finished loads waiting 231).
Reference run DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, AgentX, 8 prefill instances (DEP2) and 1 decode instance (DEP16), concurrency 6600, `max-num-seqs` 128, per-step limit 6, no in-flight cap. One hour, with lightweight CPU hooks on all 16 decode ranks and CUDA events on the worker's main stream. Average prompt ~140K tokens. - GPU step 23.1 ms, of which 1.9 ms (8%) is the GPU waiting on the CPU. Wait before forward launch: p50 0.2 ms, p90 6 ms, p99 20 ms. - 1.1 ms of that 1.9 ms is `execute_model`'s per-step DP batch-size all-reduce waiting for the slowest rank. - The last rank to reach the all-reduce is 10.5 ms behind the median rank on average (p90 21 ms). Its `schedule()` takes 10.9 ms (median rank 3.5 ms) and its `update_from_output()` 4.4 ms (1.1 ms). All 16 ranks are slowest about equally often. - `schedule()` takes 3.4 ms (p50) with no new load and ~2.8 ms more per load started: 20.5 ms at 6 loads. `update_from_output()` takes 0.9 ms with no finished request and ~2.3 ms more per finished request. - ~15.5 req/s per rank (~0.36 per step), ~0.69 s per KV load.
### E2E, before #65319 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, 7 prefill instances (DEP2) and 1 decode instance (DEP16), NIXL, AgentX at concurrency 4800, with the decode batch full: | | tok/s/GPU | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | |---|---:|---:| | no limit | 460K | 109 | | limit 4 | 516K | 153 | The decode step returned to the decode-only level (22.4 ms). These runs came from a development tree and included two smaller CPU fixes on the same admission path, so not all of the gain belongs to this change. Limit 4 beat 10-12 there. Before #65319 the limit was also the only thing holding back the pile-up of finished loads, a job the cap now does. ### Unit tests ```bash pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_kv_load_failure_recovery.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -q pre-commit run --files vllm/config/scheduler.py vllm/engine/arg_utils.py vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py ``` 324 passed on CPU, and pre-commit passes. `test_max_async_kv_loads_per_step` covers the limit alone, with the cap, and with the cap on a full batch. Restoring the previous check (`self.waiting` only) fails the two cap cases; removing the limit fails all three. This change only affects scheduling order, not model output, so there are no accuracy evals. ## Details **How a burst becomes a GPU stall:** 1. Prefill finishes and the request reaches a decode rank's waiting queue. 2. `schedule()` starts its async KV load: it allocates KV blocks for the whole prompt and moves it to `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`. It takes no running slot, so nothing but the cap limits how many start in one step. 3. Each load costs ~2.8 ms of Python on that rank. 4. The next `execute_model` does a DP all-reduce, so all 16 ranks wait for the rank that started the most. 5. The KV arrives, and the request waits for a running slot. **Why the cap alone leaves this open.** The cap only binds once `held` nears `cap`, and `cap` has to stay above rate x load time to keep up. In the reference run about 2/3 of the time was spent below `max-num-seqs`, with ~10.6 loads in progress, so a cap large enough to keep up leaves room for a burst. When the batch is full and the cap is reached, #65319 already paces loads to one per admission, and the limit adds little there. #65319's description also notes that a per-step limit could be layered on. **Implementation.** With a cap set, remote-prefill requests wait in `async_kv_waiting`, so the limit moved from a `self.waiting` check before the head is peeked to the gate shared with `_admits_inflight_kv_load()`. A head stopped by the limit behaves like one stopped by the cap: an `async_kv_waiting` head stops only that queue for the step, and a `self.waiting` head ends admission for the step. Each limited step still evaluates one head request up to that gate, as the cap already does. **Suggested settings, from this repro only:** cap around 1.5x rate x load time (16 at the reference load), and a per-step limit above the arrival rate and no larger than the typical burst. This depends on load, so the limit is a setting and not a fixed default. **Limitations:** - The repro models `schedule()` on the slowest rank, not GPU idle, and leaves out `update_from_output()`. Its numbers are not a predicted bubble reduction, and async overlap absorbs part of a late rank. - Step time does not feed back into arrivals. Load time is fixed at 30 steps, and the arrival process is synthetic. - Raising concurrency alone does not reach the high-load case. Once prefill is saturated, decode's arrival rate stops growing; it takes more prefill capacity and a larger `max-num-seqs`. - Even at limit 1, some rank starts a load on most steps, so the slowest rank stays near 6.2 ms. Lowering that needs a lower cost per load. - #64379 and #65285 (both open) remove the repeated reservation sum. Part 1 is already linear at this size (~2.7 ms per load), so they would not remove this per-load cost. **Not a duplicate:** searched open PRs for `per-step async kv` and `max_num_inflight_kv_loads`. #65319 caps loads held, and its description lists this change as an alternative and a possible layer on top. #64379 and #65285 lower the cost of an admission, not how many start in a step.

Usage, from a checkout of #61725: PYTHONPATH=. python repro_per_step_vs_inflight.py 2>/dev/null Part 1 times a real schedule() call: one step can start `cap` loads. Part 2 replays 16 DP ranks.
